svg.title: Platform as a Product
svg.desc: Platform as a Product. An internal developer platform run like a product: developers are its customers, self-service is its interface, adoption is earned. Step 1, Ticket queue, ivory tower: A ticket queue: 140 open, 9 working days to a new service, shadow scripts and a mesh nobody uses. Step 2, Developers are customers: A product manager interviews all six teams; the roadmap follows their pains and starts thin. Step 3, Self-service, measured: Self-service in minutes, with docs and support; a year on: 5 of 6 teams, 20 min, 20 tickets. Step 4, Pitfalls and limits: Pitfalls: a mandate, no PM, imagined needs, a golden cage, renamed ops, counting features shipped.

g.text: A ticket queue: 140 open, 9 working days to a new service, shadow scripts and a mesh nobody uses.
A product manager interviews all six teams; the roadmap follows their pains and starts thin.
Self-service in minutes, with docs and support; a year on: 5 of 6 teams, 20 min, 20 tickets.
Pitfalls: a mandate, no PM, imagined needs, a golden cage, renamed ops, counting features shipped.
see the platform as a gate
6 engineers · every request waits on them
every request goes through the platform team
A new service needs four tickets, one after another:
= 9 working days to a first deploy in staging
interviews with all 6 teams · a developer survey, 44 answers
one pain per quarter, in order
✗ A golden cage, or too thin
no way out for an unusual need; or only a wiki, and teams glue the rest
→ composable parts, a documented way out, grow with demand
the same people and the same ticket queue, with a new name on the door
→ self-service first; a ticket is a sign of a missing feature
“34 features this year” says nothing about use, speed or satisfaction
→ adoption, time to first deploy, satisfaction, DORA metrics
